# Model 2 (Numeric Values)

Because the first model didn't improve upon the base model all that much, I tried almost all of the numeric values. This resulted in a significantly better RMSE.

```{python}
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Read data
data = pd.read_csv('../PACFiles/analysis_data.csv')
print(data.head())
X = data.loc[:,['age', 'num_children', 'credit_score', 'owns_home', 'annual_income', 'has_auto_loan', 'num_credit_cards', 'credit_limit', 'num_transactions', 'tenure', 'avg_transaction_value', 'reward_points_balance', 'travel_frequency']]
y = data.monthly_spend
reg = LinearRegression()
reg.fit(X,y)

# Apply model
scoring_data = pd.read_csv('../PACFiles/scoring_data.csv')
scoring_data_X = scoring_data.loc[:,['age', 'num_children', 'credit_score', 'owns_home', 'annual_income', 'has_auto_loan', 'num_credit_cards', 'credit_limit', 'num_transactions', 'tenure', 'avg_transaction_value', 'reward_points_balance', 'travel_frequency']]
pred = reg.predict(scoring_data_X)

# Construct submission
submission_file = pd.DataFrame({'customer_id': scoring_data.customer_id, 'monthly_spend': pred})
submission_file.to_csv('../PACFiles/submission_file_3.csv', index=False)

from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
train_pred = reg.predict(X)
rmse = root_mean_squared_error(y, train_pred)
print("Training RMSE:", rmse)
```
